calls.output: Use the Greek yoghurt you have in the pantry in place of the sour cream. Stir in 200g off the heat, as you are doing now, and warm it very gently on the lowest heat. Yoghurt splits more easily than sour cream, so don't let it bubble.

Greek yoghurt, which the household has in the pantry, is the best swap for the sour cream. Let the pan cool for a minute, then stir in about 200g of yoghurt. Keep the heat very low, because yoghurt splits even more easily than sour cream.

Stir in about 100ml of the oat cream (the household has it) after blending, then warm it through gently on the hob without boiling. Oat cream is dairy-free, so it makes the soup silky without changing the tomato flavour much. Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed.

Oat cream is dairy-free, so it's safe for your household's restrictions, and it makes the soup silky without changing the tomato flavour much. Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed.

Stir in about 100ml of the oat cream the household has, after blending, then gently reheat without letting it boil. Oat cream is dairy-free and adds silkiness without changing the tomato flavour much. Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed.

Use the porridge oats the household has in stock: blitz or crush about 30g finely, then mix them into the bean mixture. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the oats soak up the moisture, then shape the patties. If the mixture still feels wet, add a little more oats. Chilling the patties for 10 minutes before frying will also help them hold together.

Use the porridge oats the household has in stock: blitz or crush about 30g finely, then mix them into the bean mixture. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the oats absorb the moisture, then shape the patties firmly. Chilling them for 10 minutes before frying will help them hold together in the pan.

Use the ground flaxseed the household already has: stir 2 tbsp (about 15g) into the mixture with 3 tbsp (45ml) of water, leave it for 5 minutes to thicken, then mix it in. Also drain and pat the beans dry with kitchen paper first, as excess moisture is what makes patties break. Chill the shaped patties for 10 minutes before frying if you can.

Use your largest frying pan in place of the wok for steps 2 and 3, adding a splash of vegetable oil, which you have in the pantry. Cook the chicken in two batches over high heat, about 4 minutes each, so the pan isn't crowded and the chicken browns rather than steams. Then return all the chicken with the broccoli and pepper, and stir-fry for the 3 minutes as before.

Use your largest frying pan instead of the wok for steps 2 and 3, and cook in two batches. Browning the chicken in 2 or 3 minutes per batch with a splash of vegetable oil (which your household has) stops it steaming. Keep the heat high, then stir-fry the broccoli and pepper for about 3 minutes before adding the soy sauce.

Use your largest frying pan in place of the wok for steps 2 and 3. Cook the chicken in two batches over high heat, about 5 minutes in total, so it browns rather than steams. Then stir-fry the broccoli and pepper for 3 minutes before adding the soy sauce. You have vegetable oil in the pantry, so use a splash of that to stop the chicken sticking.

Use a small splash of the white wine vinegar, which the household has in the pantry. Stir in about 1 teaspoon (5ml) with an extra ladle of the hot chicken stock, which is also in the pantry. Stir until it is absorbed, as the vinegar is sharper than wine, so keep it to that small amount.

Stir in a cornflour slurry, which the household has in the pantry and is gluten-free. Mix 1 tablespoon of cornflour with 3 tablespoons of cold water until smooth, then stir it into the simmering stew. Let it bubble gently for 2 to 3 minutes, and it will thicken.

Stir in a slurry of 1 tablespoon of cornflour mixed with 2 tablespoons of cold water, which the household has in the pantry. Pour it into the simmering stew, stirring constantly, and let it bubble for 2 minutes until it thickens. If it's still thin, repeat with a little more slurry, but check that your cornflour is labelled gluten-free.

Stir in a cornflour slurry, which the household has in the pantry. Mix 1 tablespoon (about 10g) of cornflour with 3 tablespoons of cold water until smooth. Stir it into the simmering stew and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until the sauce thickens. Cornflour is naturally gluten-free, but check the packet label to be sure.

Sprinkle on about 2 tablespoons (roughly 20g) of the sunflower seeds, which the household has in stock and are nut-free. Their light crunch goes well with the sesame oil. Scatter them over just before serving so they stay crisp.

Sprinkle on about 20g of sunflower seeds, which your household has in stock. They add a nutty-tasting crunch without being a nut, and they go well with the soy and sesame flavours. Scatter them over each serving so they stay crisp.

Sprinkle on the sunflower seeds, which the household has in the pantry and which are nut-free and peanut-free. Toast about 2 tablespoons' worth (roughly 20g) in a dry pan over a medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until golden, then scatter them over just before serving for a nutty flavour and good crunch.

The salmon is done when the flesh has turned from translucent to opaque pinkish-orange about three-quarters of the way up the side, and the fillet feels just firm when pressed. After turning, check the thickest part with the tip of a knife: the flesh should flake easily and look slightly translucent in the very centre. It will carry on cooking off the heat, so take it out at that point.

The salmon is done when the flesh has turned from translucent to opaque pinkish-orange about three-quarters of the way up the side, and the fillet feels firm with a slight spring. Peek at the thickest part with the tip of a knife: it should flake easily and be just barely translucent in the very centre. It will finish cooking from the residual heat as it rests.

The salmon is done when the flesh has turned from translucent to opaque pinkish-orange and flakes easily when you press the thickest part gently with the fish slice. You'll also see the colour change creeping up the side of the fillet during the first 4 minutes, so aim for it to be opaque almost all the way up before turning. If the centre still looks glossy and raw after 3 minutes on the second side, give it another 30 seconds.

Stir in 15 ml of coconut aminos, which the household has in the pantry and is a soy-free way to add savoury depth. Add it for the last 30 seconds so it bubbles and coats the chicken and broccoli. Taste, and add a small pinch of salt only if it still needs it.

Stir in about 15ml of coconut aminos, which your household has in the pantry. It adds salty-sweet savoury depth, and it is soy-free, so it is safe for your household. Toss it through for about 30 seconds so it coats the chicken and broccoli, then taste before adding any salt.

Stir in about 15ml of coconut aminos, which the household has in the pantry. It adds savoury depth without soy. Toss it through the hot wok for 30 seconds so it clings to the chicken and broccoli, then taste before adding any salt.

Use hot water flavoured with the white miso paste your household has in stock: stir about 1 tablespoon of miso into 1 L of hot water, tasting as you go. Keep it hot on the hob so it doesn't stop the rice cooking. Miso is salty, so hold back on adding any extra salt until the end.

Use the white miso paste the household has: stir about 1 tablespoon (15g) into 1 litre of very hot water until dissolved, then keep adding it a ladle at a time as before. If you want extra depth, the dried porcini can be soaked in that water first, but the miso alone will do. Taste before adding any salt, as miso is already salty.

Use the white miso paste the household has: whisk about 1 tbsp (15g) into 1 litre of hot water in the saucepan until dissolved. Keep it hot and carry on adding it a ladle at a time. Taste before adding any salt, as miso is already salty.

Jah, suurus on oluline: sammudes 3 ja 4 peavad kartulid ja kanakoivad mahtuma ühe kihina, muidu kartulid aurustuvad ega pruunistu. Jaga kõik kahele väiksele ahjuplaadile või ahjuvormile, pane need ahju eri riiulitele ja vaheta nende kohad 20 minuti pärast, küpsetusaeg ja 200 °C jäävad samaks. Kontrolli lõpus, et kana sisetemperatuur on 75 °C.

Jah, suurus on oluline: sammus 3 peavad kartulid ja kanakoivad mahtuma ühe kihina, muidu kartulid aurustuvad sammus 4 ega pruunistu. Jaga need kahe ahjukindla vormi või plaadi vahele ja küpseta sammus 4 mõlemat korraga ahju kahel restil, ajaga 45 minutit. Vaheta vormide kohad poole aja pealt, siis pruunistub kõik ühtlaselt.

Jah, suurus on oluline: sammudes 3 ja 4 peavad kartulid ja kanakoivad mahtuma ühe kihina, muidu kartulid hauduvad, mitte ei pruunistu. Jaga 1250 g kartuleid ja 5 kanakoiba kahe väikese plaadi vahel ära ning pane plaadid eri riiulitele. Vaheta plaatide kohad umbes 22 minuti pärast, küpsetusaeg jääb samaks, 45 minutit.
